stem:
A 74-year-old woman with urosepsis is brought to the emergency department lethargic and confused. Examination shows cool extremities, delayed capillary refill, and a blood pressure of 80/50 mm Hg with a heart rate of 118 beats per minute.

Which of the following values best approximates her mean arterial pressure?

options.label: A
options.misconception: Diastolic pressure alone is being reported as the mean.
options.explanation: MAP adds one-third of the pulse pressure to diastolic; 50 mm Hg ignores the systolic contribution during the brief systolic phase.

options.label: B
options.explanation: Mean arterial pressure equals diastolic plus one-third of the pulse pressure: 50 + 30/3 = 60 mm Hg, consistent with hypotensive shock.

options.label: C
options.misconception: The arithmetic midpoint of systolic and diastolic is being used.
options.explanation: The simple midpoint of 80 and 50 is 65 mm Hg; MAP weights diastole more heavily and gives about 60 mm Hg.

options.label: D
options.misconception: Two-thirds of the pulse pressure is being added instead of one-third.
options.explanation: Adding two-thirds of the pulse pressure to diastolic overestimates MAP; the correct computation yields about 60 mm Hg.

options.label: E
options.misconception: Systolic pressure is being reported as the mean.
options.explanation: Systolic pressure is the peak, not the time-averaged perfusion pressure; MAP is much closer to diastolic in hypotension.

context: Learning objective: compute MAP in shock. MAP = diastolic + (systolic − diastolic)/3; values below about 65 mm Hg threaten organ perfusion.
